$comment: Facts for the home-page Fact Shuffler (replaces spotifyPlaylists). headline = catchy display line; body = the fact in plain prose, 50+ words each; category = small mono label. One is shown at random on load; 'next fact' cycles randomly without repeating until all are seen (tracked in sessionStorage), then resets.

items.headline: The loudest sound in recorded history
items.body: When Krakatoa erupted in 1883, the explosion was so violent it produced the loudest sound ever recorded by human instruments. People heard it nearly 5,000 kilometers away in Australia, mistaking it for cannon fire. The blast also sent a pressure wave that circled the entire globe, and sensitive barometers as far as London registered it passing by seven separate times over the following days.

items.headline: A day longer than a year
items.body: Venus rotates so slowly on its axis that it takes about 243 Earth days to spin around once, yet it only takes roughly 225 Earth days to complete a full orbit around the Sun. That means a single day on Venus, measured from sunrise to sunrise, technically lasts longer than an entire Venusian year — a strange quirk of orbital mechanics found nowhere else in the solar system.

items.headline: Cleopatra was closer to the Moon landing
items.body: The pyramids at Giza were already ancient monuments by the time Cleopatra was born, having been built around 2560 BCE. Cleopatra actually lived closer in time to the launch of Apollo 11 and the first Moon landing in 1969 than she did to the construction of the Great Pyramid. Less time separates her from astronauts walking on the Moon than separates her from ancient Egypt's own early history.

items.headline: Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire
items.body: Teaching is believed to have begun at Oxford University as early as 1096, making it one of the oldest institutions of higher learning in the world. The Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan, which would later become Mexico City, was not founded until 1325 — more than two centuries after Oxford's earliest recorded classes. Students were already sitting through tutorials while the Aztec Empire had yet to exist.

items.headline: The Great Wave is not a painting
items.body: Katsushika Hokusai's Great Wave off Kanagawa is one of the most recognizable images in art history, yet it was never a painting at all. It is a woodblock print, part of a series called Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, and thousands of copies were mass-produced and sold cheaply to ordinary people. Its striking deep blue color came from Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment newly imported from Europe.

items.headline: France spans twelve time zones
items.body: Thanks to its scattered overseas territories — from French Polynesia in the Pacific to French Guiana in South America — France technically spans more time zones than any other country on Earth, a total of twelve. That is more than Russia and the United States cover with their own vast territories, despite mainland France being a fairly modest size compared to those two much larger nations.

items.headline: Space smells like seared steak
items.body: Astronauts who have completed spacewalks consistently describe a strange, distinct smell clinging to their suits and equipment once they re-enter the airlock. Many compare it to hot metal, gunpowder, or seared steak. Scientists believe the scent comes from atomic oxygen reacting with the suit's exterior materials and then off-gassing once exposed to a breathable atmosphere again — essentially the smell of space itself, experienced secondhand.

items.headline: The animal that ages backwards
items.body: The tiny jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii has an extraordinary ability that almost no other known animal shares: when injured, aging, or starving, it can revert its mature cells back into an earlier juvenile state, effectively restarting its entire life cycle from scratch. Because it can repeat this transformation indefinitely under the right conditions, biologists often call it the closest thing to a biologically immortal animal on the planet.

items.headline: A war shorter than a lunch break
items.body: The Anglo-Zanzibar War, fought between the United Kingdom and the Sultanate of Zanzibar on the morning of August 27, 1896, is officially recognized as the shortest war in recorded history. It lasted somewhere between 38 and 45 minutes from the first shot to the surrender, triggered by a succession dispute after the death of the previous sultan — shorter than most people's lunch break at work.

items.headline: Saudi Arabia imports camels from Australia
items.body: Camels are not native to Australia, but the country is now home to the largest population of wild dromedary camels anywhere on Earth. They descend from camels imported in the 1800s to help explore the outback before cars and railways existed. Today, Australia exports some of these camels — descendants of the originals — back to Middle Eastern countries like Saudi Arabia, completing an unlikely round trip.

items.headline: The Night Watch was cropped like a bad thumbnail
items.body: Rembrandt's The Night Watch is one of the most celebrated paintings in art history, but the version hanging in the Rijksmuseum today isn't quite what he originally painted. In 1715, when the painting was moved to Amsterdam's town hall, it was physically trimmed on all four sides to fit a smaller space between two doors — permanently removing two entire figures from the left edge of the composition.

items.headline: Switzerland can shelter its entire population
items.body: Switzerland's long-standing civil defense laws once required that shelter space be available for every single resident of the country, whether in private basements, apartment buildings, or dedicated public facilities. As a result, the country maintains enough nuclear-hardened bunker capacity to shelter more people than actually live there — a level of civil preparedness that remains largely unmatched anywhere else in the world today.

items.headline: The Sahara was green
items.body: As recently as six thousand years ago, during a period known as the African Humid Period, the Sahara desert looked nothing like it does today. It was covered in lakes, rivers, and grasslands, home to hippos, crocodiles, and giraffes. Rock art discovered deep in some of the driest, most inhospitable parts of the modern desert still depicts people swimming and herding cattle across a landscape that has since vanished.

items.headline: The loneliest place on Earth
items.body: Point Nemo, located in the South Pacific Ocean, is the point on Earth farthest from any land — roughly 2,700 kilometers from the nearest coastline in any direction. It's so remote that the closest humans are often astronauts aboard the International Space Station passing overhead, rather than anyone on a boat. Space agencies have used the area as a designated graveyard for decommissioned spacecraft for decades.

items.headline: Everyone you know fits in one pixel
items.body: In February 1990, as it was leaving the solar system, the Voyager 1 spacecraft turned its camera around and photographed Earth from about six billion kilometers away. In that image, the entire planet — every person who has ever lived — appeared as less than a single pixel of light suspended in a sunbeam. Astronomer Carl Sagan later called it the 'pale blue dot,' a phrase that stuck.

items.headline: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer
items.body: The Eiffel Tower is built almost entirely of iron, a material that expands when heated and contracts when cooled. On a hot summer day, the tower can stand as much as 15 centimeters taller than it does on a cold winter morning, purely from thermal expansion of its iron lattice structure. Engineers accounted for this natural movement when the tower was originally designed back in 1889.

items.headline: Octopuses run on three hearts
items.body: Octopuses have three hearts instead of one. Two of them pump blood specifically to the gills, while the third circulates it to the rest of the body. Their blood is also blue rather than red, because it uses a copper-based protein called hemocyanin to carry oxygen instead of the iron-based hemoglobin found in humans, which works better in the cold, low-oxygen conditions of deep ocean water.

items.headline: Honey basically never goes bad
items.body: Archaeologists have discovered pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, sealed for over three thousand years, that were still perfectly edible when opened. Honey's extremely low moisture content and naturally acidic pH create an environment where bacteria and microorganisms simply cannot survive or multiply. That is why, if stored properly and kept sealed, honey is one of the only foods on Earth that essentially never spoils.

items.headline: Everest is still growing
items.body: Mount Everest isn't a fixed height — it is actually still growing, by roughly 4 millimeters every year, as the ongoing collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates continues to push the Himalayas upward. At the same time, the mountain also shifts slightly sideways due to that same plate movement, meaning its exact summit position is technically different today than it was even a decade ago.

items.headline: Only one animal poops in cubes
items.body: Wombats are the only known animals in the world that produce cube-shaped droppings. Researchers eventually discovered that this unusual shape comes from variations in the elasticity of different sections of the wombat's intestine during the final stages of digestion, rather than any special shaping mechanism. Scientists believe the flat-sided droppings are less likely to roll away, helping the animals mark territory more effectively on uneven ground.

items.headline: Bananas are berries, strawberries aren't
items.body: Botanically speaking, a berry is a fruit produced from a single flower with one ovary, containing seeds embedded in its flesh — a definition that bananas satisfy perfectly, along with grapes, tomatoes, and avocados. Strawberries, on the other hand, are technically 'accessory fruits' because the fleshy part doesn't develop from the ovary at all — the real fruits are the tiny seed-like specks dotting their surface.
